deep.reconstruction:
Context. On the previous page Hilbert sketches an algebraic construction of algebraic functions (Riemann surfaces) with prescribed branch points. He counts constants, then varies the coefficients of the Φ_i using the 'Satz von der Functionaldeterminante' (an implicit/inverse-function theorem) so that any prescribed branch point α can be reached. He then begins a proof of that theorem: (1) find a path running in the finite part of the plane on which the discriminant of the problem behaves suitably. The transcription says it 'becomes = 0'; the sense almost certainly requires that it stays ≠ 0, so the Jacobian is invertible along the path. This page continues with an analytic-continuation argument along that path, which I parametrize as t ∈ [0,1]. Call a point t 'good' if a 'Darstellung' (a solution, i.e. a representation of the unknowns as analytic functions of the parameters) exists at t.

(2) Closedness from the left. Suppose all points t' < t arbitrarily close to t are good. Then t is good. In modern terms, if t_n ↑ t and each t_n is good, the solutions converge to a solution at t. So the set of good points is closed under left limits.

(3) Openness via power series. If t_0 is good, the power-series expansion (implicit-function theorem with nonvanishing functional determinant) gives a neighbourhood (t_0 − δ, t_0 + δ) consisting of good points. So the good set is open in the path.

Conclusion. Start at t = 0, which is good. Claim: the whole path can be traversed. Suppose there were bad points. Bisect, keep the half in which the first bad points lie, and iterate (nested intervals, Bolzano–Weierstrass). This produces a point P with the following property: every point left of P is good, and right of P there are bad points arbitrarily close to P. In modern terms, P = sup{s : [0,s] consists of good points}.

[Implicit, mine:] By (2), P is good. By (3), a whole neighbourhood of P is then good, contradicting the existence of bad points arbitrarily close to the right of P. Hence every point of the path is good, and the solution continues along the entire path. This is a connectedness / 'method of continuity' argument for analytic continuation of implicit solutions.
errors: Step (2) is asserted without justification. Passing to the limit needs a uniform bound or compactness for the solutions, plus nondegeneracy of the functional determinant at the limit point. Neither is stated here; presumably this is the role of the discriminant condition in step (1).
The bisection is described only tersely ('so nehme ich die Mitte'). The rule for which half to keep is not stated, though the intended construction (supremum of the initial good segment) is clear.
The final contradiction, which combines (2) and (3) at P, is not written on the page; the argument breaks off once P is constructed.
Previous-page step (1) as transcribed reads 'Diskriminante ... r=0 wird'. Logically it must mean that the discriminant (Jacobian) does not vanish on the path; either a slip or a transcription issue.

results.what: Continuation of solutions of an implicit analytic system along a path by an open/closed (connectedness) argument, using the power-series implicit function theorem for openness and a limit argument for closedness
results.modern_name: Method of continuity / analytic continuation along a path via the implicit function theorem (connectedness of [0,1])
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit-function power series: Cauchy (1831), Weierstrass. Continuity method in existence proofs: Klein and Poincaré in the 1880s, later S. Bernstein.

results.what: Bisection producing a boundary point P separating good from bad points
results.modern_name: Nested-interval / Bolzano–Weierstrass bisection (least upper bound argument)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard lecture-note style continuity/bisection argument for analytic continuation of implicit solutions, embedded in a sketch of an existence theorem for algebraic functions with prescribed branching. It is routine 19th-century material with no new mathematical content.

checkable.asserts: Implicit-function derivative formula dy/dx = -F_x/F_y, the basis of the local power-series continuation in step (3); should simplify to 0.
The discriminant 4 - 27*x**2 vanishes exactly where F_y = 0 has a common root with F, i.e. where local continuation can fail. This illustrates why the path must avoid zeros of the discriminant.
Example of the local power-series 'Darstellung' near a regular point (y = sqrt(1+x) = 1 + x/2 - x**2/8 + ...), as invoked in step (3).
